structured_output.hypothesis: If domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species, then dog genomes will show substantial ancestry from, or paraphyly with respect to, more than one wild canid species, and not nest wholly inside a single one.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using whole-genome assemblies and reads for Canis lupus familiaris and wild Canis/canid species (gray wolf, coyote, golden jackal, Ethiopian wolf, African golden wolf), dogs show one of the following. (a) Dog nuclear genomes carry ancestry from at least two distinct wild species, each contributing at least 10% of genome-wide ancestry. This is measured by ADMIXTURE or f4/D-statistics, with |Z| > 3 for each non-wolf source. (b) Dog lineages are polyphyletic across at least two reciprocally monophyletic wild-species clades, with bootstrap support of 90% or more.
structured_output.fail_criterion: All dog genomes fall within a single wild species' clade, which is Canis lupus (gray wolf). Any non-wolf canid contributes less than 2% genome-wide ancestry (D-statistics |Z| < 3 or ancestry fraction < 2%), and dogs form a monophyletic group nested within gray wolf variation with 90% or more bootstrap support.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'wild species' means distinct biological species, a rank he treated loosely, and his 'several' means two or more. 'Descended from' is read as genetic ancestry of the domestic dog gene pool. It is tested by phylogenetic placement of dog genomes relative to wild Canis species, and by admixture and introgression statistics. Under the modern reading, a single domestication from an extinct or extant gray wolf population, with later minor gene flow, would count as refuting Darwin's multi-species claim. Gene flow below 2% would not count as descent from several species. Dog-wolf crossing does not count either, because the wolf is one species.

dataset.name: NCBI Genome: Canis lupus familiaris (taxid 9615) genome assemblies
dataset.publisher: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), U.S. National Library of Medicine
dataset.why_it_fits: The NCBI Datasets portal lists downloadable genome assemblies (FASTA, GFF) for the domestic dog. The same portal, queried by taxon, gives assemblies for gray wolf (taxid 9612), coyote (Canis latrans, 9614), golden jackal (Canis aureus, 9611) and related canids. Whole-genome alignment and SNP calling across these assemblies would allow admixture, f4/D-statistic and phylogenetic analysis. The fields used are the assembly accession, organism name and sequence files. The test would check dogs' placement relative to wild species and the fraction of ancestry from non-wolf species.
